title: Effect of pressure on the magnetic properties of (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$
authors: Tamás Prok, Zoltán Kovács-Krausz, Harvey Stanfield, Bing Zhao, Michael Leonárd Morgan, Bálint Fülöp, Marcos H. D. Guimarães, Ivan J. Vera-Marun, Saroj Prasad Dash, Szabolcs Csonka, Péter Makk, Endre Tóvári
abstract: Cobalt-doped Fe$_5$GeTe$_2$ possesses a rich magnetic phase diagram as a function of Co concentration. The nature of magnetic order in (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$ is especially interesting, as it has been shown to exhibit ferromagnetic order, A-type antiferromagnetic (AFM) order, or potentially both at the same time. Here we present magnetoresistance measurements on antiferromagnetic (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$ at a series of pressures and extract the anisotropy and interlayer exchange fields using the two-sublattice model. We show a 50 % increase of the interlayer exchange at 2 GPa, highlighting the sensitivity of magnetic properties to interlayer distance. In addition, we find that the sharp hysteretic transitions observed within the AFM state can be qualitatively described by a linear chain model, which suggests an even-odd effect as a function of layer number instead of a coexisting ferromagnetic phase.
summary: This work experimentally and theoretically investigates how hydrostatic pressure modifies the complex magnetic order of (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$. By analyzing magnetoresistance, the researchers quantified that pressure strongly enhances interlayer coupling while successfully modeling subtle AFM hysteresis using a linear chain approach, suggesting surface effects dominate over bulk FM coexistence.
main_problem: The study investigates how external pressure tunes the magnetic properties of (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$, specifically focusing on understanding the nature of its magnetic order within the Antiferromagnetic (AFM) state.
main_result: Applying pressure significantly enhances the interlayer exchange coupling ($J$) by about 50% at 2 GPa, and the small hysteresis loops observed in the AFM phase are explained by surface layer behavior modeled via a linear chain approach rather than coexisting ferromagnetic order.
method: The research combines magnetoresistance measurements (Hall effect) under varying pressures with theoretical modeling using both two-sublattice and linear chain models to extract magnetic parameters.
model_or_system: The physical system is the 2D magnet (Co$_{0.5}$Fe$_{0.5}$)$_5$GeTe$_2$. The analysis employs the two-sublattice model for bulk behavior and a linear chain model to describe layer-dependent phenomena, such as surface layer switching.
key_observables: Magnetoresistance ($R_{xy}$) vs. magnetic field ($H$), Spin-flop transition field ($	ext{H}_{	ext{SF}}$), small hysteresis loops within the AFM state, and interlayer exchange coupling ($J$).
important_parameters: Applied pressure ($p$) up to 2 GPa; anisotropy constant ($K$); interlayer exchange coupling ($J$); layer number ($N$).
main_assumptions: The small hysteresis loops are attributed solely to surface layer switching described by the linear chain model, avoiding the need for a coexisting FM phase. The analysis often involves fitting data using simplified two-sublattice approximations.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM/optical images and $R_{xy}$ vs. $H$ curves at various pressures and temperatures; subsequent figures plot derived fields ($	ext{H}_{	ext{SF}}$) versus pressure or temperature, and analyze the ratio of hysteresis features ($\Delta R / \Delta r / N$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from presenting experimental measurements of magnetoresistance under pressure to applying theoretical models (two-sublattice and linear chain) to fit the data. It systematically analyzes phase transitions ($	ext{SF}$ vs $	ext{FM}$) and finally uses the chain model to explain fine details like small hysteresis loops.
why_interesting: The ability to tune magnetic interactions ($J$) by external pressure, combined with modeling layer-by-layer magnetism using concepts from quantum many-body physics (like chain models), provides insights into emergent quantum phenomena in 2D materials.
